tracks.title: Command Line Basics
tracks.audience: Complete beginners who have never opened a terminal window. Start here if typing commands to a computer is new to you.

slides.heading: Meet the terminal
slides.lede: The command line looks intimidating, but it is just a faster way to talk to your computer — in words instead of clicks.
slides.narration: Welcome to the command line. In this lecture you will learn what a terminal is, what a shell is, and run your first three commands.

slides.heading: What a command line is
bullets: A terminal is a text window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons and menus.
A shell is the program inside the terminal that reads your commands and runs them. On Linux and macOS it is usually bash or zsh; on Windows it is PowerShell.
You type a command, press Enter, and the computer prints its answer back as text.
Almost everything you can do by clicking — opening files, creating folders, running programs — can also be done by typing.
You do not need to memorize hundreds of commands. Five or six cover most everyday work.
slides.narration: A terminal is a text window, and the shell inside it runs your typed commands. Typing plus Enter is the whole interaction model, and a handful of commands covers most daily work.

slides.heading: Anatomy of a command

diagram.title: Anatomy of a command
diagram.note: Most commands follow one pattern: name, then options starting with a dash, then the thing to act on — all separated by spaces.

slides.narration: Nearly every command has the same shape: a name, optional flags that start with a dash, and an argument naming the target. Learning this pattern once makes every new command easier to read.

slides.heading: Your first three commands

code.code:
$ whoami
alex

$ date
Sun Oct  4 11:52:00 EDT 2026

$ echo hello
hello

slides.walkthrough: whoami prints your username. date prints the current date and time. echo repeats whatever you type after it. The $ is the prompt — the shell prints it to say it is ready, and you never type it yourself.
slides.narration: Three safe commands to start with: whoami tells you who you are, date tells you the time, and echo repeats your words. The dollar sign is the shell's prompt, not something you type.

slides.heading: Try it: say hello
slides.text: Open a terminal on your machine (Terminal on macOS, the Terminal app on Linux, or PowerShell on Windows). Type `echo hello` and press Enter. You should see `hello` printed back at you.
slides.narration: Open a terminal and run echo hello. If you see hello printed back, your terminal works and you have run your first command.

slides.heading: Getting help without fear
slides.lede: Nobody memorizes the command line. Professionals look things up constantly — here is how.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches the two built-in help systems every command carries, so you never have to guess what a command does.

slides.heading: How to read a command
bullets: Options change a command's behavior: -l often means long format, -r often means recursive, -h often means human-readable.
Most commands answer --help. Typing `ls --help` prints a short summary of what the command does and its options.
Longer commands have a manual page: `man ls` opens the full documentation. Press q to quit the manual.
Inside a manual page, type / and a word to search for it, then press n to jump to the next match.
When stuck, read the error message first. It usually names the exact problem, like a missing file or a typo.
slides.narration: Every command documents itself through --help and manual pages. Learning to read those two sources is more valuable than memorizing any single command.

slides.heading: Asking a command for help

code.code:
$ ls --help
Usage: ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...
List information about the FILEs
...

$ man ls
LS(1)              User Commands              LS(1)
NAME
       ls - list directory contents
...

slides.walkthrough: --help gives a quick reminder of usage and the most common options. man opens the complete manual with every option explained in detail. Skim the NAME and DESCRIPTION sections first; the EXAMPLES section, when present, is the fastest way to learn.
slides.narration: The --help flag gives a quick usage reminder, while man opens the full manual. The NAME line tells you what the command does in one sentence.

slides.heading: The help workflow

diagram.title: The help workflow
diagram.note: Quick reminder first, full manual second, search inside it, then quit. This loop answers most command-line questions.

slides.narration: The help workflow is a loop: start with --help for a reminder, escalate to man for detail, search within it, and quit when answered.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Typing the prompt character $ yourself. It is printed by the shell; you only type what comes after it.
Forgetting to press Enter. Nothing happens until you do — the shell waits for that keypress.
Panicking at an error. Errors are instructions, not verdicts; read them slowly, one line at a time.
Copy-pasting commands with curly smart quotes instead of straight quotes. They look the same but the shell rejects them.
slides.narration: The most common beginner mistakes are typing the prompt character, forgetting Enter, and fearing error messages. All four pitfalls here are easy to spot once you know they exist.

slides.heading: Try it: read a manual
slides.text: Run `man echo` (or `echo --help` on Windows PowerShell, try `Get-Help echo`) and find the one-sentence description of what the command does. Press q to exit the manual when you are done.
slides.narration: Practice the help workflow: open a manual page, find the one-sentence description, and quit. This is the habit working professionals use dozens of times a day.

tracks.title: Linux Command Line
tracks.audience: Beginners comfortable opening a terminal who need real Linux skills: navigating files, reading text, and chaining commands with pipes.

lectures.title: Files, folders, and where you are

slides.heading: Files, folders, and where you are
slides.lede: Linux keeps every file in one big tree. Learn to walk it and you will never feel lost.
slides.narration: This lecture maps the Linux filesystem and teaches the four navigation commands you will use every day: pwd, ls, and cd.

slides.heading: The Linux filesystem
bullets: Everything starts at the root directory, written as /. Folders hang off it like branches of a tree.
Your personal files live in your home directory, such as /home/alex. The shell shortens this to ~.
pwd prints where you are right now (print working directory). It is your compass.
ls lists what is in the current folder. cd <folder> moves you into a folder. cd .. steps back up one level.
Paths starting with / begin at the root (absolute). Paths without a leading / begin where you are now (relative).
slides.narration: Linux organizes everything as one tree rooted at slash. Your home folder is your personal branch, and pwd, ls, and cd are how you move through the tree.

slides.heading: The directory tree

diagram.title: The directory tree
diagram.note: Folders nest inside folders. Everything hangs off the single root /, and /home/alex is where your files live.

slides.narration: Picture the filesystem as a tree: the root at the top, system folders like etc and var on their own branches, and your home folder holding everything personal.

slides.heading: Moving around

code.code:
$ pwd
/home/alex

$ ls
docs  photos  notes.txt

$ cd docs
$ pwd
/home/alex/docs

$ cd ..
$ pwd
/home/alex

slides.walkthrough: pwd shows the current folder. ls lists its contents: two folders and one file. cd docs moves into docs, and pwd confirms the new location. cd .. moves back up one level to /home/alex.
slides.narration: Watch pwd and cd work together: pwd answers where am I, ls answers what is here, and cd moves you. The double dot always means one level up.

slides.heading: Try it: explore home
slides.text: Use pwd to confirm you are in your home folder, then ls to see what is there. Pick one subfolder, cd into it, and come back out with cd ..
slides.narration: Practice the navigation loop: confirm with pwd, look with ls, move with cd, and step back with cd dot-dot.

slides.heading: Reading and shaping text
slides.lede: Logs, configs, and data are all text. These five tools let you read, search, and count any of it.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces the text toolkit: cat, head, tail, grep, sort, uniq, and wc — the commands behind most log reading and data shaping.

slides.heading: The text toolkit
bullets: cat prints a whole file. less lets you scroll through it page by page (press q to quit).
head shows the first 10 lines of a file; tail shows the last 10. Add -n 20 to see 20 lines instead.
grep searches for a word inside files: `grep error app.log` prints every line containing error.
sort orders lines; uniq removes adjacent duplicates. They are usually paired: `sort file | uniq`.
wc counts things: lines with -l, words with -w, bytes without a flag.
slides.narration: Five tools read and shape text: cat and less for viewing, head and tail for edges, grep for searching, sort and uniq for ordering, and wc for counting.

slides.heading: Searching a log file

code.code:
$ cat app.log
INFO starting up
ERROR disk full
INFO retrying
ERROR disk full
INFO shutting down

$ grep ERROR app.log
ERROR disk full
ERROR disk full

$ grep -c ERROR app.log
2

slides.walkthrough: cat dumps the whole log. grep ERROR keeps only the lines containing the word ERROR. grep -c counts matching lines instead of printing them, answering how many errors happened with a single number.
slides.narration: A typical debugging session in three commands: view the file, filter to the interesting lines, then count them. This pattern answers most what went wrong questions.

slides.heading: The pipe idea

diagram.title: The pipe idea
diagram.note: The | pipe character feeds one command's output into the next command's input, chaining small tools into big jobs.

slides.narration: The pipe is the command line's superpower: it connects commands so the output of one becomes the input of the next, like an assembly line for text.

slides.heading: Try it: search something
slides.text: Pick any text file on your system (try /etc/hosts on Linux or macOS). Run grep on it for a common word like `local` and count the matches with grep -c.
slides.narration: Practice searching a real file with grep, then counting matches with grep -c. Searching before reading is the professional habit.

slides.heading: Redirecting and chaining commands
slides.lede: Pipes connect commands to each other; redirection connects them to files. Together they build real workflows.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches pipes, output redirection, and command chaining — the combination behind almost every real shell workflow.

slides.heading: Pipes and redirection
bullets: | (pipe) sends a command's output into another command's input.
> writes output into a file, replacing it. >> appends to the end of a file instead.
< feeds a file's contents into a command as its input.
&& runs the next command only if the first one succeeded. A plain ; runs it regardless.
2> redirects error messages separately from normal output, useful when a command is noisy.
slides.narration: Pipes connect commands to each other, while angle brackets connect commands to files. The double ampersand chains commands so each step only runs if the last one worked.

slides.heading: A real pipeline

code.code:
$ grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c > errors.txt

$ cat errors.txt
      2 ERROR disk full

$ echo "checked" >> errors.txt && echo done
done

slides.walkthrough: grep finds the error lines, sort orders them, uniq -c counts the repeats, and > saves the report into errors.txt instead of printing it. Then >> appends the word checked, and && prints done only because the append succeeded.
slides.narration: Here is a complete workflow: filter, sort, count, and save — one line. Then append a note and confirm success, all chained together.

slides.heading: The error-report pipeline

diagram.title: The error-report pipeline
diagram.note: Each stage transforms the text and hands it to the next. The final redirect saves the report instead of printing it.

slides.narration: This flow diagram is the pipeline from the code slide: filter to errors, sort them, count repeats, and save the report to a file.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Using > when you meant >> wipes a file's contents. Remember: single > replaces, double >> appends.
Forgetting quotes around text with spaces. File names containing spaces must be wrapped in quotes.
Piping into a command that does not read input. For example, ls | cd does nothing because cd never reads stdin.
Getting Permission denied on a redirect. Check who owns the file with ls -l before assuming the command is wrong.
slides.narration: The classic disasters are wiping a file with a single greater-than sign and piping into commands that ignore input. Both are easy to avoid once you have seen them named.

slides.heading: Try it: build a pipeline
slides.text: Chain three commands: list your home folder with ls, search that listing for one letter with grep, and save the result into a file called matches.txt. Then cat the file to check your work.
slides.narration: Build your first three-stage pipeline: list, filter, and save. Reading the saved file back confirms each stage did its job.

tracks.title: YAML from Zero
tracks.audience: Beginners who will read or write configuration files for tools like Kubernetes, Ansible, Docker Compose, or CI pipelines.

slides.heading: YAML from zero
slides.lede: YAML is how modern tools store their settings — plain text that both humans and machines can read.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces YAML: why it exists, how indentation creates structure, and your first working example.

slides.heading: Why YAML exists
bullets: YAML is a way to write structured data — settings, lists, configurations — that humans can read at a glance.
Tools like Kubernetes, Ansible, Docker Compose, and CI pipelines all read YAML files.
It uses indentation with spaces (never tabs) to show what belongs inside what.
A colon marks a key-value pair: `name: alex` means the key name holds the value alex.
Comments start with # and are ignored. Use them to explain your config to future you.
slides.narration: YAML stores structured settings as readable text. Indentation shows nesting, colons mark key-value pairs, and hash signs start comments.

slides.heading: Your first YAML

code.code:
server:
  host: example.com
  port: 8080
  enabled: true

# a simple list lives under 'tags'
tags:
  - web
  - prod

slides.walkthrough: server is a map holding three keys. Indentation nests host, port, and enabled inside server. enabled: true is a boolean, port: 8080 is a number. The dashed lines under tags form a list of two strings.
slides.narration: This small example shows everything: a nested map, a boolean, a number, a comment, and a two-item list. Read the indentation to see the structure.

slides.heading: Indentation is nesting

diagram.title: Indentation is nesting
diagram.note: Deeper indentation means inside the thing above. Every level must use the same number of spaces.

slides.narration: Think of indentation as a family tree: deeper lines are children of the line above. Consistent spacing is what makes the structure unambiguous.

slides.heading: Try it: describe yourself
slides.text: Write a YAML snippet describing yourself: a name, a city, and a list of two hobbies. Check that every nested line is indented by exactly two spaces.
slides.narration: Write your own tiny YAML document. If every nested line sits two spaces deeper than its parent, a parser will read it exactly as you intended.

slides.heading: Lists, maps, and nesting
slides.lede: Real configs nest lists inside maps inside lists. Learn the two building blocks and you can read any of them.
slides.narration: This lecture goes deeper: lists of maps, maps inside lists, and how to tell which is which at a glance.

slides.heading: Two building blocks
bullets: A map is key-value pairs: `name: web`. Order usually does not matter, names must be unique.
A list is an ordered sequence of items, each starting with a dash and a space: `- web`.
A list item can itself be a map. The dash starts the item; the indented keys below it belong to that item.
A map value can be a list. Put the key on one line, then indent the dashed items beneath it.
Blank lines are ignored, so use them to visually separate sections.
slides.narration: Maps and lists are the only two structures in YAML. Everything complex is just these two nested inside each other.

slides.heading: A list of maps

code.code:
services:
  - name: web
    image: web:v1
    ports:
      - 80
      - 443
  - name: db
    image: db:v2

slides.walkthrough: services holds a list of two items. Each dash starts one service, which is a map with name, image, and (for web) ports. The web service's ports value is itself a list of two numbers, indented under ports.
slides.narration: Read this inside out: services is a list, each item is a map describing one service, and the web service's ports are a nested list. Three levels, two building blocks.

slides.heading: YAML versus JSON

diagram.title: YAML versus JSON
diagram.note: YAML and JSON describe identical structures. YAML trades punctuation for whitespace to stay readable.

slides.narration: YAML and JSON are two spellings of the same data. If you can read a JSON object, you already understand YAML's maps and lists.

slides.heading: Try it: two servers
slides.text: Write YAML for a key called `servers` holding a list of two servers. Each server is a map with `name` and `ip` keys. Keep the dashes and indentation aligned.
slides.narration: Practice the most common real-world shape: a named list of maps. Getting the dash and indentation alignment right here pays off in every config file you will ever write.

slides.heading: YAML gotchas that bite everyone
slides.lede: Four small rules cause nearly every YAML error. Learn them once and config files stop being scary.
slides.narration: This lecture covers the four traps that break YAML files: tabs, the boolean trap, colon spacing, and quoting.

slides.heading: The big four
bullets: Tabs are forbidden. Indent with spaces only — a single tab character anywhere is an error.
In YAML 1.1, the words yes, no, on, and off parse as booleans. Quote them ('yes') if you mean the literal word.
A colon must be followed by a space: `key: value` works, `key:value` does not.
Strings with special characters need quotes: `message: "hi: there"` keeps the colon inside the value.
Consistent indentation depth matters. Pick two spaces per level and never mix depths.
slides.narration: Tabs, unquoted yes and no, missing space after colons, and mixed indentation cause almost every YAML failure. Four rules, memorized once, prevent them all.

slides.heading: Broken versus fixed

code.code:
# BROKEN: tab indentation + missing space
server:
	host:example.com

# FIXED: spaces + space after colon
server:
  host: example.com
  notify: "yes"

slides.walkthrough: The broken version uses a tab and writes host:example.com with no space — both are errors. The fixed version uses two spaces and a space after each colon. notify is quoted so the word yes stays a string instead of becoming boolean true.
slides.narration: Compare the broken and fixed versions line by line. Every difference is one of the big four rules.

slides.heading: The YAML debug loop

diagram.title: The YAML debug loop
diagram.note: Every YAML error message points at a line number. Go there first; the mistake is almost always indentation or a missing space.

slides.narration: When YAML breaks, do not stare at the whole file. Validate it, read the reported line number, and check indentation and colon spacing on that line.

slides.heading: Try it: spot the bug
slides.text: This snippet has one bug — find it: `app:` newline ` name:shop` newline ` port:8080`. (Hint: check what follows each colon.) Then rewrite it correctly.
slides.narration: Find the single spacing bug in the broken snippet, then rewrite it correctly. Spotting these quickly is the skill this whole track builds.

tracks.title: Networking Fundamentals
tracks.audience: Beginners who need the core ideas behind every networked system: addresses, DNS, ports, and HTTP.

slides.heading: What a network is
slides.lede: A network is just computers that can reach each other — and every cloud, website, and app you will study sits on top of one.
slides.narration: This lecture defines networks, packets, and IP addresses — the three ideas everything else in networking builds on.

slides.heading: Networks in one minute
bullets: A network is two or more computers linked so they can exchange data. The internet is the biggest one.
Data travels in small chunks called packets. Each packet carries a destination address and a piece of the message.
An IP address is a numeric label identifying a device on a network, like a street address for computers.
IPv4 addresses look like 192.168.1.10: four numbers (octets), each 0 to 255, separated by dots.
Devices called routers forward packets toward their destination, hop by hop, until they arrive.
slides.narration: Computers exchange data as packets, each labeled with a destination IP address. Routers forward those packets hop by hop across networks until they arrive.

slides.heading: A packet's journey

diagram.title: A packet's journey
diagram.note: Packets hop from device to device. No single wire connects you to the server; routers chain the path together.

slides.narration: Follow one packet from your computer to a server: it hops through your router, across the internet, through their router, and finally arrives. Every web page you load takes this trip.

slides.heading: Checking the path with ping

code.code:
$ ping -c 3 example.com
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=55 time=18.2 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=1 ttl=55 time=17.9 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

slides.walkthrough: ping sends small echo-request packets and times the replies. The address in parentheses is the server's IP. time=18.2 ms is the round trip — lower is faster. 0% packet loss means every packet made it there and back.
slides.narration: Ping is the simplest network test: it sends echo packets and reports how long the round trip took. Zero percent loss and low milliseconds mean a healthy path.

slides.heading: Try it: ping something
slides.text: Run `ping -c 3 example.com` in your terminal. Read the time values — that is how many milliseconds a round trip to that server takes from where you sit.
slides.narration: Ping a real server and read the round-trip times. Those milliseconds are the physical distance of the internet, measured.

slides.heading: DNS: the internet's phone book
slides.lede: Humans remember names like example.com. Computers need numbers like 93.184.216.34. DNS translates between them.
slides.narration: This lecture explains the Domain Name System: the hierarchical lookup that turns every name you type into an IP address.

slides.heading: How DNS works
bullets: DNS is a distributed directory that maps domain names to IP addresses.
It is hierarchical: root servers know where .com lives, .com servers know where example.com lives, and example.com's servers give the final address.
Your computer asks a resolver (usually run by your ISP or a public service) which walks this chain for you.
Answers are cached at every level, so repeat visits skip most of the chain and resolve fast.
If DNS fails, names stop resolving — the internet still works, but you cannot find anything by name.
slides.narration: DNS walks a hierarchy from root to top-level domain to the domain itself, caching answers along the way. When DNS breaks, the internet feels broken even though packets still flow.

slides.heading: A DNS lookup, step by step

diagram.title: A DNS lookup, step by step
diagram.note: Each layer answers one smaller question. Caching means most lookups only touch the first one or two layers.

slides.narration: Each layer of DNS answers a smaller question than the last, narrowing down from the root to the exact address. Caching short-circuits this chain for names you visit often.

slides.heading: Looking up a name yourself

code.code:
$ nslookup example.com
Server:         192.168.1.1
Address:        192.168.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:   example.com
Address: 93.184.216.34

slides.walkthrough: nslookup asks your resolver for a name's address. The Server lines show which resolver answered. The Address line is the answer: example.com currently lives at 93.184.216.34.
slides.narration: The nslookup command performs a DNS lookup on demand. The last line is the answer your browser would use to connect.

slides.heading: Try it: compare two sites
slides.text: Run nslookup on two different websites and compare their addresses. Notice that big sites may return different addresses on repeat lookups — that is load balancing, not an error.
slides.narration: Look up two sites and compare. Seeing multiple addresses for one name is normal: large sites spread traffic across many servers.

slides.heading: Ports and services
slides.lede: An IP address finds the machine. A port number finds the program on that machine.
slides.narration: This lecture explains ports: how one server runs many services, the famous port numbers, and TCP versus UDP.

slides.heading: Ports in one minute
bullets: A port is a 16-bit number (0 to 65535) identifying a specific program on a machine.
The IP address gets the packet to the computer; the port number gets it to the right program.
Famous ports are standardized: 80 is HTTP, 443 is HTTPS, 22 is SSH, 53 is DNS, 25 is SMTP email.
You rarely type ports because software assumes the defaults: browsers use 443 for https:// automatically.
A port only accepts traffic if a program is listening on it. Closed ports simply refuse the connection.
slides.narration: Ports let one machine run dozens of services at one address. The famous numbers — 80, 443, 22, 53 — are conventions every professional recognizes.

slides.heading: Reading host:port

code.code:
https://example.com:443
|_____| |___________| |__|
scheme      host        port

https://example.com      (port 443 implied)
http://example.com:8080  (non-standard port shown)

slides.walkthrough: A full address has three parts: the scheme (https), the host (example.com), and the port (443). Default ports are implied and usually hidden; you only write the port when a service uses a non-standard one, like 8080.
slides.narration: Addresses are scheme, host, and port. Defaults stay invisible; unusual ports are written out explicitly after a colon.

slides.heading: TCP versus UDP

diagram.title: TCP versus UDP
diagram.note: Web pages and files use TCP. Live video and games use UDP, where speed beats perfection.

slides.narration: TCP guarantees every packet arrives in order, like a phone call. UDP fires packets off with no promises, like postcards — faster, but some may never arrive.

slides.heading: Try it: name that port
slides.text: From memory, match each port to its service: 80, 443, 22, 53. Then think: which port does your browser use when you visit an https:// site?
slides.narration: Quiz yourself on the four famous ports. Recognizing 80, 443, 22, and 53 on sight is a genuine professional skill.

lectures.title: HTTP: the language of the web

slides.heading: HTTP: the language of the web
slides.lede: Every page, image, and API call on the web is an HTTP conversation: a request, then a response.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches HTTP requests and responses: methods, status codes, and how to inspect a real conversation with curl.

slides.heading: Requests and responses
bullets: HTTP is a request/response protocol: the client asks, the server answers. HTTPS is the same conversation, encrypted.
Methods say what you want: GET reads, POST submits, PUT replaces, DELETE removes.
Every response carries a status code. The first digit tells the story: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx your mistake, 5xx their mistake.
200 means OK, 404 means not found, 403 means forbidden, 500 means the server crashed handling your request.
Headers are metadata on both sides: content type, caching rules, authentication tokens.
slides.narration: HTTP is a simple dialogue: the client makes a request with a method, and the server replies with a status code and content. The status code's first digit tells you who is at fault when something breaks.

slides.heading: One page load

diagram.title: One page load
diagram.note: Every page load is one or more of these cycles. Images, styles, and scripts each trigger their own request.

slides.narration: A page load is a cycle: request, processing, response, render. Modern pages repeat this cycle dozens of times for images, styles, and scripts.

slides.heading: Watching HTTP with curl

code.code:
$ curl -sI https://example.com | head -5
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
content-length: 1256
date: Sun, 04 Oct 2026 15:52:00 GMT
server: ECS

slides.walkthrough: curl -I asks for just the response headers. HTTP/2 200 is the status line: protocol plus success. content-type says this is an HTML page. The rest is metadata the server volunteers about its answer.
slides.narration: The curl command lets you watch raw HTTP. The status line and content-type header tell you whether the request worked and what kind of data came back.

slides.heading: Try it: read a status line
slides.text: Run `curl -sI https://example.com` and find the status code. Then try a nonsense path like `curl -sI https://example.com/nope` and watch the code change.
slides.narration: Fetch headers for a real page and a missing page. Seeing 200 become 404 makes status codes concrete instead of abstract.

tracks.title: Identity & Access Concepts
tracks.audience: Beginners who need the mental model behind every login system and cloud permission: users, groups, roles, and policies.

lectures.title: Users, groups, and why they exist

slides.heading: Users, groups, and why they exist
slides.lede: Every permission system answers one question: who is allowed to do what? It starts with identity.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces identities: users, groups, and the habit of attaching permissions to groups instead of people.

slides.heading: Identity basics
bullets: An identity is a who: a person, or sometimes a program acting on its own.
A user is a long-lived identity, usually one per human, with its own credentials.
A group bundles users together so you can manage them as one unit: developers, operators, interns.
Permissions attach to groups, not to people. People join and leave groups; the permissions stay put.
Least privilege: give every identity only the access it actually needs, and nothing more.
slides.narration: Users identify people, groups bundle them, and permissions attach to the groups. Least privilege — nothing more than needed — is the rule behind every good setup.

slides.heading: Attach permissions to groups

diagram.title: Attach permissions to groups
diagram.note: When Priya changes teams, you move her between groups. No permissions are edited, so nothing is forgotten.

slides.narration: Groups sit between people and permissions. Moving a person between groups updates everything they can do in one step, with no stale access left behind.

slides.heading: A tiny access map

code.code:
developers  ->  read/write code repos
operators   ->  restart servers, read logs
interns     ->  read-only dashboards

alex: developers
priya: developers, operators
sam: operators

slides.walkthrough: Three groups each hold a bundle of permissions. Alex is a developer, Sam is an operator, and Priya sits in both groups, so she gets both bundles. Nobody's permissions are written next to their name.
slides.narration: This access map shows the pattern: permissions live on groups, and people collect permissions by membership. Priya's two memberships combine.

slides.heading: Try it: design groups
slides.text: Sketch your own tiny organization: three users and two groups. Decide which permissions each group holds and who belongs where.
slides.narration: Design groups for a fictional team. Deciding where permissions live is the core skill of access management.

slides.heading: Roles: borrowing permission
slides.lede: Users are who you are. Roles are hats you put on temporarily — powerful, then gone.
slides.narration: This lecture explains roles: temporary identities you assume, why they beat permanent keys, and where you will meet them.

slides.heading: Roles in one minute
bullets: A role is an identity with permissions attached, but nobody logs in as it directly.
Instead, a user or program assumes the role and receives temporary credentials, often lasting minutes to hours.
When the credentials expire, the power evaporates. There is no permanent key to steal.
Common uses: an app reading files from storage, an admin elevating for a sensitive task, one account helping another.
A trust policy controls who is allowed to assume the role in the first place.
slides.narration: Roles hand out short-lived power instead of permanent keys. Assuming a role, doing the task, and letting the credentials expire is the safe pattern.

slides.heading: Assuming a role

diagram.title: Assuming a role
diagram.note: The power is borrowed, never owned. Expiry is automatic, so forgotten keys cannot linger.

slides.narration: Assuming a role is a five-step dance: request, receive temporary credentials, act, and let them expire. Nothing permanent is ever created.

slides.heading: User versus role

code.code:
user:  alex
  credentials: password (long-lived)
  power: whatever alex's groups allow

role:  backup-writer
  credentials: temporary token (expires in 1h)
  power: write backup files, nothing else

nightly job -> assumes backup-writer -> writes -> done

slides.walkthrough: Alex the user has a long-lived password and broad group permissions. The backup-writer role has a narrow job and one-hour credentials. The nightly job assumes the role, writes backups, and the power vanishes when the hour ends.
slides.narration: Compare the permanent user with the temporary role: narrow power, short life, no password to leak. Jobs and apps should almost always use roles.

slides.heading: Try it: spot the role
slides.text: Think of one task in your own life or work that currently uses a permanent key or password but should use temporary access instead. Write down what the role would be allowed to do and how long it should last.
slides.narration: Find a permanent credential in your own world that deserves to be temporary. Naming the role and its expiry is how access design starts.

slides.heading: Policies: allow and deny
slides.lede: Policies are the rule documents that say exactly what an identity may do. Learn to read one and you can audit any system.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches policy documents: allow versus deny, the anatomy of a rule, and the mistakes that cause real breaches.

slides.heading: Policy basics
bullets: A policy is a document listing what an identity is allowed (or denied) to do.
Policies attach to users, groups, or roles. The identity's effective power is the combination.
Rules name an action (what), a resource (which thing), and an effect (allow or deny).
An explicit deny always beats an allow. Deny is the emergency brake.
The * wildcard means everything: powerful in the wrong place, useful in narrow ones.
slides.narration: Policies are rule lists attached to identities. Allow grants power, deny overrides everything, and wildcards demand respect.

slides.heading: Reading a policy
slides.walkthrough: Effect: Allow grants permission. Action names exactly one operation: reading an object. Resource scopes it to one bucket's contents, with * matching every file under reports/. This identity can read those files and do nothing else.
slides.narration: This real-style policy allows exactly one action on exactly one set of files. Reading Effect, Action, and Resource tells you the whole story.

slides.heading: How a request is judged

diagram.title: How a request is judged
diagram.note: Deny is checked first and always wins. Without a matching allow, the default answer is deny.

slides.narration: Every request runs this gauntlet: an explicit deny stops it cold, a matching allow lets it through, and silence means no.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Overbroad wildcards: Action * on Resource * is full admin power. Never grant it by accident.
Forgetting that an explicit deny overrides every allow. One deny can silently block a whole workflow.
Scoping the resource too loosely, like a whole storage account when one folder would do.
Assuming a policy grants access the service itself would refuse. Policies can only narrow, never widen, what is possible.
slides.narration: Real breaches come from these four mistakes: wildcards too broad, forgotten denies, loose resource scoping, and assuming policies can grant the impossible.

slides.heading: Try it: extend the policy
slides.text: In one sentence, describe what the example policy allows. Then decide: what second Action would you add so the identity can also list the bucket's contents (hint: the action is called s3:ListBucket)?
slides.narration: Describe the example policy's power in your own words, then extend it with a second action. Editing policies deliberately is the skill behind every access review.

tracks.title: Python from Zero
tracks.audience: Complete programming beginners who need to read and write small Python scripts before tackling data, cloud, or AI paths.

slides.heading: Your first script
slides.lede: Python reads almost like English. Three lines are enough to write, run, and understand your first program.
slides.narration: This lecture runs your first Python program: printing text, storing values in variables, and running a file.

slides.heading: Python in one minute
bullets: Python is a programming language prized for readability: its code looks close to plain English.
print() displays text on the screen. Whatever you put inside the parentheses appears as output.
A variable stores a value under a name: `name = "Alex"` keeps the text Alex available as name.
You run a file with `python3 app.py`. Python reads your code top to bottom and executes each line.
Text values are called strings and sit in quotes. Numbers need no quotes.
slides.narration: Python's readability makes it the standard first language. Print shows output, variables store values, and python3 runs your file top to bottom.

slides.heading: Hello, variables

code.code:
name = "Alex"
print("Hello,", name)

count = 3
print(count + 4)

slides.walkthrough: Line 1 stores the string Alex in name. Line 2 prints Hello, followed by the variable's value. Line 4 stores the number 3 in count, and line 5 prints 7, because + adds numbers together.
slides.narration: Two variables, two prints. Strings join with commas in print, numbers add with plus — the same symbol does different jobs depending on the type.

slides.heading: How Python runs your code

diagram.title: How Python runs your code
diagram.note: Python is interpreted: it runs your code directly, with no separate compile step.

slides.narration: Python skips the compile step other languages need. The interpreter reads each line and runs it immediately, which makes experimenting fast.

slides.heading: Try it: change the name
slides.text: Save the example as hello.py, run it with `python3 hello.py`, then change the name to your own and run it again. Watch the output change.
slides.narration: Edit and re-run: the fastest learning loop in programming. Change one value, run, and observe.

slides.heading: Decisions and repetition
slides.lede: Programs get interesting when they can choose and repeat. That is two ideas: if and for.
slides.narration: This lecture adds branching with if and else, and repetition with for loops — the two structures behind nearly all logic.

slides.heading: Choosing and repeating
bullets: if tests a condition. The indented block under it runs only when the condition is true.
else catches everything the if missed. elif (else-if) tests a second condition in between.
Indentation is not style in Python — it defines which lines belong to the if or the loop.
for repeats a block once per item: `for name in ["a", "b"]` runs twice.
range(n) produces the numbers 0 through n-1, handy for counting loops.
slides.narration: If chooses, for repeats, and indentation shows what belongs inside each. Range gives you clean counting without manual bookkeeping.

slides.heading: A loop and a decision
slides.walkthrough: The loop runs three times with i set to 0, 1, then 2, printing each. Then score is 85, so score >= 90 is false, the if block is skipped, and the else block prints not an A.
slides.narration: Trace it: the loop prints three lines, then the condition fails and the else branch runs. Indentation is what ties each print to its block.

slides.heading: A loop, visualized

diagram.title: A loop, visualized
diagram.note: The indented body repeats once per value, then the program continues after the loop.

slides.narration: A loop is a cycle: set the variable, run the body, repeat. When the values run out, the program moves on past the loop.

slides.heading: Try it: squares
slides.text: Write a for loop using range(1, 6) that prints the square of each number (i * i). You should see 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
slides.narration: Write a loop that prints squares from 1 to 25. Getting the range bounds right is the exercise.

slides.heading: Functions and files
slides.lede: Functions package reusable logic. Files let programs remember. Together they build real scripts.
slides.narration: This lecture defines functions with def and return, and reads files with open — the two tools behind most practical scripts.

slides.heading: Functions and files
bullets: def names a reusable block: `def greet(name):` creates a function taking one input, called a parameter.
return sends a value back to the caller. Without return, a function gives back nothing.
open("notes.txt") opens a file for reading. The with block closes it automatically when done.
f.read() pulls the whole file contents into one string. len() measures how long it is.
Call a function by its name with parentheses: greet("Alex") runs the block with name set to Alex.
slides.narration: Functions wrap logic you can reuse; files persist data beyond one run. Def plus return defines the first, open plus with handles the second.

slides.heading: A function that reads a file

code.code:
def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()

print(greet("Alex"))
print(len(text), "characters read")

slides.walkthrough: greet takes a name and returns a greeting string. The with block opens notes.txt, reads it into text, and closes the file safely. The prints show the greeting and how many characters were read.
slides.narration: This script defines a function, reads a file, and reports both results. It is a complete, realistic small program in eight lines.

slides.heading: Calling a function

diagram.title: Calling a function
diagram.note: Definition stores the recipe; the call runs it. Return is how the answer travels back to the caller.

slides.narration: Functions have two moments: definition stores the recipe, the call runs it. The return value is the finished dish handed back.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Forgetting return. The function runs, but the caller receives nothing and the result vanishes.
Indentation slips. One misaligned line can move code in or out of a function silently.
File not found. open() looks in the folder where you run the script, not where the script file lives.
range() stops one short. range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 — never 3. This off-by-one bites everyone.
slides.narration: The classic beginner bugs: missing returns, drifting indentation, wrong working directory, and range stopping one early. Expect all four; recognize them fast.

slides.heading: Try it: double it
slides.text: Write a function called double that takes a number n and returns n * 2. Then print double(21) — you should see 42.
slides.narration: Define double, call it with 21, and confirm 42. A working function you wrote yourself is the milestone this track builds toward.

tracks.title: SQL from Zero
tracks.audience: Beginners who need to read data from databases: tables, SELECT queries, filtering, and sorting.

slides.heading: Tables: rows and columns
slides.lede: A database is a collection of tables, and a table is just rows and columns — a spreadsheet with rules.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces the relational model: databases, tables, columns with types, and the primary key that identifies each row.

slides.heading: The relational model
bullets: A database holds many tables. Each table stores one kind of thing: customers, orders, products.
A table is rows and columns. Columns define the shape; each row is one record.
Every column has a type: text for names, numbers for prices, dates for timestamps, true/false for flags.
A primary key is the column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row, like a customer id.
NULL means missing or unknown — it is not zero, and it is not an empty string.
slides.narration: Tables store one kind of thing as rows; columns with strict types define the shape. Primary keys identify rows, and NULL marks the unknown.

slides.heading: Anatomy of a table

diagram.title: Anatomy of a table
diagram.note: Columns define the shape and types; rows hold the actual data, one record per row.

slides.narration: See the table as a grid with rules: the header row defines typed columns, and every data row must fit that shape.

slides.heading: A table, drawn

code.code:
customers
+----+-------+--------+
| id | name  | city   |
+----+-------+--------+
|  1 | Alex  | Boston |
|  2 | Priya | Austin |
|  3 | Sam   | Boston |
+----+-------+--------+
id is the primary key: no two rows share one.

slides.walkthrough: Three columns: id (number, primary key), name (text), city (text). Three rows, each a customer. The id values 1, 2, 3 are unique — that uniqueness is what makes id a primary key.
slides.narration: This text drawing is exactly how query results look. The id column's uniqueness is the primary key doing its job.

slides.heading: Try it: design a table
slides.text: Sketch a table for your bookshelf. Pick three columns, choose a type for each (text, number, or date), and decide which column is the primary key.
slides.narration: Design a tiny table yourself: columns, types, and a primary key. Every database you will ever query started as a sketch like this.

slides.heading: SELECT: asking questions
slides.lede: SQL is a language for asking questions about data. The first question is always: show me this table.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches the SELECT statement: choosing columns, choosing tables, and reading the results.

slides.heading: The SELECT statement
bullets: SELECT names the columns you want. FROM names the table they come from.
SELECT * means all columns. Useful for exploring, wasteful in production code.
Statements end with a semicolon. SQL ignores extra whitespace and line breaks.
Column names and keywords are usually case-insensitive, but string values are not.
Read a query inside-out: FROM picks the table first, then SELECT picks the columns.
slides.narration: SELECT columns FROM table is the whole basic query. Read it inside-out — table first, columns second — and every query becomes readable.

slides.heading: Your first query

code.code:
SELECT name, city
FROM customers;

slides.walkthrough: FROM customers picks the table. SELECT name, city keeps only those two columns, dropping id. The result is a new table with two columns and all three rows.
slides.narration: This query returns every customer's name and city, dropping the id column. Two clauses, one question answered.

slides.heading: What SELECT does

diagram.title: What SELECT does
diagram.note: FROM chooses the rows, SELECT chooses the columns. The database does the scanning; you describe the shape you want.

slides.narration: Think of a query as a filter on the table's shape: FROM grabs the rows, SELECT trims the columns, and the result is a fresh table.

slides.heading: Try it: select everything
slides.text: Write a query that returns all columns from a table called orders. Then write one that returns only the total column.
slides.narration: Practice the two basic shapes: everything with star, and one column by name. These cover most exploratory queries.

slides.heading: Filtering and sorting
slides.lede: Real questions have conditions: which customers, in what order, how many? WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT answer them.
slides.narration: This lecture adds filtering with WHERE, sorting with ORDER BY, and capping results with LIMIT.

slides.heading: Narrowing the answer
bullets: WHERE filters rows: only rows matching the condition appear in the result.
Comparisons use = , <>, <, >, <=, >=. Text values go in single quotes: city = 'Boston'.
ORDER BY sorts the result by a column. Add DESC for descending, largest first.
LIMIT caps how many rows come back. LIMIT 5 returns at most five rows.
Clause order is fixed: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT ...
slides.narration: WHERE keeps matching rows, ORDER BY sorts them, LIMIT caps the count. The clause order never changes, so queries stay readable.

slides.heading: Filtered, sorted, capped

code.code:
SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Boston'
ORDER BY name
LIMIT 5;

slides.walkthrough: FROM picks customers. WHERE keeps only rows where city equals Boston. ORDER BY name sorts those survivors alphabetically. LIMIT 5 returns at most five. Each clause narrows the previous result.
slides.narration: Four clauses, one precise question: the first five Boston customers, alphabetically. Each line refines the answer a step further.

slides.heading: The clause pipeline

diagram.title: The clause pipeline
diagram.note: Each clause shrinks or orders the previous result. The order of clauses is fixed and always the same.

slides.narration: Clauses run as a pipeline: take the table, keep matching rows, sort them, then cap the count. Fixed order, predictable results.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: SQL uses a single = for comparison. == is a syntax error in most databases.
Text values need single quotes. WHERE city = Boston (no quotes) fails because Boston looks like a column name.
WHERE comes before ORDER BY. Swapping them is a syntax error.
Forgetting the semicolon. One statement can span many lines, but it needs its terminator.
NULL never equals anything, not even NULL. Filtering missing values needs IS NULL, a topic for later.
slides.narration: The classic SQL mistakes: double equals, unquoted text, swapped clause order, and treating NULL like an ordinary value.

slides.heading: Try it: Austin, alphabetically
slides.text: Write a query returning the name column from customers, keeping only rows where city is 'Austin', sorted by name.
slides.narration: Combine WHERE and ORDER BY in one query. This exact shape — filter then sort — appears in real work constantly.

tracks.title: Cloud Concepts
tracks.audience: Beginners who need the mental model behind AWS, Azure, and OCI: regions, services, billing, and who is responsible for what.

slides.heading: Regions and availability zones
slides.lede: The cloud is just someone else's data centers — organized into regions and zones you choose between.
slides.narration: This lecture explains regions and availability zones: the geography of the cloud and why placement matters.

slides.heading: Cloud geography
bullets: A region is a geographic area containing cloud data centers, like us-east-1 in Virginia or eu-west-1 in Ireland.
An availability zone (AZ) is one or more isolated data centers inside a region, with independent power and networking.
Deploying across multiple AZs keeps your app running when one data center fails.
Pick regions close to your users: distance becomes latency, and latency becomes slowness.
Some services are regional (one copy per region); some are global (one copy worldwide).
slides.narration: Regions are places, zones are isolated buildings within them. Spreading across zones buys resilience; choosing nearby regions buys speed.

slides.heading: One region, three zones

diagram.title: One region, three zones
diagram.note: Zones fail independently but act as one region. Your app runs in two or more; if one goes dark, the others carry on.

slides.narration: A region is a cluster of independent zones. Running your app in several zones means one building's bad day is not your outage.

slides.heading: Choosing a region

code.code:
users in Boston  ->  us-east-1 (Virginia): ~10 ms away
users in Boston  ->  eu-west-1 (Ireland): ~80 ms away

region = "us-east-1"   # pick once, close to your users
deploy to zones a, b, c # survive one zone failing

slides.walkthrough: Virginia is a short hop from Boston; Ireland is an ocean away. Region choice is a latency decision you make once. Zone choice is a resilience decision you make per deployment.
slides.narration: Region is about distance to users; zones are about surviving failure. Both choices are made up front and rarely revisited.

slides.heading: Try it: place an app
slides.text: Your users are in Boston and your backup team is in Austin. Which US region would you shortlist for the app, and how many zones would you deploy to?
slides.narration: Practice the placement decision: near the users, across multiple zones. This reasoning applies to every cloud provider.

slides.heading: The service menu
slides.lede: Every cloud sells the same three things in different packaging: compute, storage, and network.
slides.narration: This lecture tours the service categories: compute, storage, networking, and managed databases.

slides.heading: Compute, storage, network
bullets: Compute runs your code: virtual machines, containers, or serverless functions that run on demand.
Storage holds your data: object storage for files, block disks for databases, file shares for shared folders.
Networking connects it all: virtual private networks, load balancers, and DNS.
Managed databases (relational, NoSQL, caches) trade control for freedom from patching and backups.
Service names hint at their category: EC2 is compute, S3 is storage, VPC is network.
slides.narration: Every cloud app is some mix of compute, storage, and network. Managed services sell you the same pieces with the maintenance included.

slides.heading: The cloud stack

diagram.title: The cloud stack
diagram.note: Your app sits on compute, compute reads storage, and the network ties every piece together.

slides.narration: Picture the stack as layers: your app on top, compute running it, storage holding its data, and networking connecting all three.

slides.heading: Reading a service name

code.code:
EC2, Azure VMs, OCI Compute   -> runs your code (compute)
S3, Blob Storage, Object Storage -> holds files (storage)
VPC, VNet, VCN                   -> private network (network)
RDS, Azure SQL, MySQL HeatWave   -> managed database

slides.walkthrough: Different providers, same categories. Once you can sort any service into compute, storage, network, or database, every provider's hundred-service menu becomes navigable.
slides.narration: Provider names differ; categories do not. Sorting services into compute, storage, network, or database is the skill that transfers across clouds.

slides.heading: Try it: sort the workload
slides.text: Match each need to a category: run a web app, store nightly backups, give servers a private network, keep user accounts queryable.
slides.narration: Sort four everyday needs into compute, storage, network, or database. This categorization is the first step of every cloud design.

slides.heading: Billing and shared responsibility
slides.lede: The cloud bills by the sip, and security is split down the middle. Both surprise beginners — neither has to.
slides.narration: This lecture covers pay-as-you-go billing and the shared-responsibility model: what the provider secures versus what you secure.

slides.heading: Pay as you go
bullets: The cloud bills for what you use: compute hours, gigabytes stored, requests served, data transferred.
Resources you forget to delete keep billing. A test server left running all month is a real invoice line.
Billing dimensions differ per service: learn the two or three that apply to what you launched.
Set billing alerts early. A $10 alert teaches the same lesson as a $1,000 surprise, cheaper.
Tags and labels let you attribute costs to teams and projects when the bill arrives.
slides.narration: Cloud billing rewards attention: know what you launched, alert on spend, and delete what you no longer need.

slides.heading: Shared responsibility

diagram.title: Shared responsibility
diagram.note: The provider secures the cloud itself; you secure what you put in it. More managed services move the line toward the provider.

slides.narration: Security is split: the provider guards the physical cloud, you guard everything you deploy in it. The line shifts with how managed the service is.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Leaving test resources running. The number one beginner cloud bill is a forgotten experiment.
No billing alerts. Set them on day one, before you need them.
Assuming the cloud backs up your data for you. Backups are your responsibility unless a managed service promises them.
Wide-open access rules. A storage bucket readable by the whole internet is a breach waiting for a scanner.
slides.narration: The expensive mistakes are all avoidable: forgotten resources, missing alerts, assumed backups, and open access. Check all four before you deploy anything real.

slides.heading: Try it: draw the line
slides.text: List two things the cloud provider always handles and two things that are always yours, for a virtual machine you rent.
slides.narration: Draw the responsibility line for a virtual machine yourself. Knowing exactly where your duties start prevents both neglect and duplicated effort.

tracks.title: Programming Basics
tracks.audience: Absolute beginners who have never written code: what code is, how programs run, variables, input, and output.

slides.heading: What code actually is
slides.lede: Code is a set of instructions written in a language both humans and computers can follow.
slides.narration: This lecture defines code, programs, and programming languages — the vocabulary every later track assumes.

slides.heading: Code in one minute
bullets: Code is instructions written in a programming language: text files a computer can execute.
A program is code that does something when run: a calculator, a website, a game.
Programming languages differ in style and strengths, not in magic. Python, Java, C, and JavaScript all express the same ideas.
A program is data plus logic: values it works with, and instructions for what to do with them.
You do not need math genius to start. You need patience and a willingness to experiment.
slides.narration: Code is written instructions, a program is those instructions running, and languages are stylistic choices over shared ideas. Data plus logic is the whole game.

slides.heading: From idea to running program

diagram.title: From idea to running program
diagram.note: Code is the bridge between an idea and a running program. Everything else is detail.

slides.narration: Every program travels the same road: an idea becomes text, the text runs, and a result appears. Learning to program is learning to write that middle step.

slides.heading: The smallest program

code.code: print(2 + 3)

slides.walkthrough: print displays a value. 2 + 3 is arithmetic the computer evaluates first, giving 5. Running this prints the single character 5. One line, one idea, one result.
slides.narration: The smallest real program: print a sum. The computer evaluates the arithmetic, then displays the answer.

slides.heading: Try it: program versus document
slides.text: In one sentence, describe what a program does that a document does not. (Hint: think about what happens when each one runs.)
slides.narration: Distinguish programs from documents in your own words. A program acts; a document sits — that difference is the starting point.

slides.heading: How programs run
slides.lede: Your code becomes machine action through layers: interpreters, operating systems, and the CPU itself.
slides.narration: This lecture explains how code executes: machine instructions, compiled versus interpreted languages, and the layers in between.

slides.heading: From text to action
bullets: The CPU only understands machine instructions: tiny operations like add these numbers or jump there.
Compiled languages translate your whole file into machine code before running. C and C++ work this way.
Interpreted languages run your code line by line through an interpreter. Python and JavaScript work this way.
The operating system manages resources: memory, files, and which program runs when.
Memory holds your program's data while it runs. Turn off the power and RAM forgets everything.
slides.narration: CPUs run machine instructions; compilers and interpreters bridge your text to those instructions; the operating system manages the resources programs share.

slides.heading: The execution layers

diagram.title: The execution layers
diagram.note: Each layer translates for the one below it. You write for the top; the bottom does the work.

slides.narration: Four layers turn your text into action: your code, a translator, the operating system, and the hardware. Bugs can hide at any layer, but beginners live at the top.

slides.heading: Two paths to running

code.code:
app.py  ->  python3  ->  runs now        (interpreted)
app.c   ->  gcc      ->  app  ->  runs    (compiled)

slides.walkthrough: Python source runs immediately through the interpreter: one step. C source goes through the compiler gcc first, producing a machine-code file called app, which then runs: two steps. Interpreted is faster to try; compiled is faster to run.
slides.narration: Interpreted languages run in one step, compiled languages in two. The tradeoff is iteration speed versus execution speed.

slides.heading: Try it: which is which
slides.text: Answer from what you learned: is Python interpreted or compiled? What about C? Say why the difference matters when you are experimenting.
slides.narration: Classify Python and C, and explain why interpreted languages suit experimentation. Naming the tradeoff shows you understood the layers.

slides.heading: Variables, input, and output
slides.lede: Variables remember, input listens, output speaks. These three are the senses of every program.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches variables, reading input, printing output, and the types that decide what + means.

slides.heading: Remember, listen, speak
bullets: A variable is a named box holding a value: `city = "Boston"` stores text under the name city.
Assignment uses a single =. It stores the right side's value into the left side's name.
input() pauses and reads a line the user types, always returning text.
print() displays values. Text and numbers print the same way; combining them has rules.
Types matter: + adds numbers but joins text. Mixing them without converting is an error.
slides.narration: Variables store, input reads, print shows. The type of a value — text or number — decides what operations like plus are allowed to do.

slides.heading: Input, variables, output

code.code:
name = input("Your name? ")
print("Hello, " + name)

age = 30
print(age + 1)

slides.walkthrough: input asks for a name and stores the typed text in name. The first print joins Hello, with that text. age holds the number 30, so age + 1 is arithmetic and prints 31.
slides.narration: This program listens, remembers, and speaks: it reads a name, greets it, then does arithmetic on a number. Text joins, numbers add.

slides.heading: Same symbol, different types

diagram.title: Same symbol, different types
diagram.note: The type decides what + does. Mixing types without converting is an error in most languages.

slides.narration: Plus joins text but adds numbers. The type of the values — not the symbol — decides the operation.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Adding text to a number. "30" + 1 fails; convert first or keep types consistent.
Forgetting quotes around text. Boston without quotes looks like a variable name.
Confusing = (store a value) with == (compare two values). One assigns, the other asks.
Typos in variable names. Python treats name and naem as two different variables.
slides.narration: The beginner classics: mixing types, forgetting quotes, confusing assignment with comparison, and typos that create phantom variables.

slides.heading: Try it: three lines
slides.text: Write three lines: store your city in a variable, store a number in another variable, and print both on one line.
slides.narration: Write a three-line program using two variables and one print. Small programs that work beat big programs that do not.

tracks.title: HTTP & the Web
tracks.audience: Beginners heading into web development: how browsers work, URLs, status codes, and what APIs are.

slides.heading: The browser's journey
slides.lede: Loading a page looks instant. Underneath, your browser runs a six-step relay race every single time.
slides.narration: This lecture follows a page load from keystroke to pixels: DNS, connection, request, response, and rendering.

slides.heading: What happens when you press Enter
bullets: You type a URL. The browser parses it into scheme, host, path, and query.
DNS translates the host name into an IP address so the browser knows where to connect.
The browser opens a connection to the server, encrypted with TLS when the scheme is https.
It sends an HTTP request: method, path, headers, and sometimes a body.
The server replies with a status code, headers, and the page content. The browser renders it.
Images, styles, and scripts each trigger their own request/response cycle.
slides.narration: A page load is a relay: parse, resolve, connect, request, respond, render. Each leg can fail independently, which is why knowing the steps helps you debug.

slides.heading: One page load

diagram.title: One page load
diagram.note: A modern page repeats the request/response part dozens of times for its images, styles, and scripts.

slides.narration: Six steps, repeated per resource. Slowness can hide in any step, so professionals learn to measure each one.

slides.heading: Try it: count the requests
slides.text: Open your browser's developer tools (F12), switch to the Network tab, and reload any page. Count how many requests one page load actually makes.
slides.narration: Watch the relay race live in the Network tab. The request count surprises everyone the first time.

slides.heading: URLs, methods, and status codes
slides.lede: URLs name things, methods say what you want, and status codes report what happened. Three vocabularies, one conversation.
slides.narration: This lecture dissects URLs, HTTP methods, and the status code families you will read for the rest of your career.

slides.heading: Methods and status codes
bullets: Methods say what you want: GET reads, POST submits, PUT replaces, DELETE removes.
Status codes report the outcome. The first digit tells the story of who is at fault.
2xx means success (200 OK). 3xx means redirect: look over there instead.
4xx means your mistake: 404 not found, 403 forbidden, 401 unauthorized.
5xx means their mistake: 500 internal server error, 503 service unavailable.
slides.narration: Methods express intent, status codes report results. The first digit of the code tells you whether to fix your request or wait for the server.

slides.heading: Anatomy of a URL

code.code:
https://shop.example.com/search?q=boots#top
|___|  |______________| |_____| |__| |__|
scheme       host          path  query fragment

slides.walkthrough: https is the scheme: encrypted HTTP. shop.example.com is the host to connect to. /search is the path: which resource. ?q=boots is the query: parameters for the request. #top is the fragment: handled by the browser, never sent to the server.
slides.narration: Every URL has the same five parts. The query carries parameters, and the fragment never leaves your browser.

slides.heading: Status code families

diagram.title: Status code families
diagram.note: Read the first digit. It tells you whether the request worked, moved, was wrong, or the server broke.

slides.narration: Four families cover every outcome. When debugging, the first digit decides your next move: retry, fix the URL, or escalate.

slides.heading: Try it: diagnose
slides.text: Two scenarios: you see a 404, then a 500. For each, say in one sentence what happened and whose fault it is.
slides.narration: Practice reading status codes as diagnoses. 404 is yours to fix; 500 is theirs to fix.

slides.heading: APIs: programs talking to programs
slides.lede: An API is a menu for programs: order data in a fixed format, get data back in a fixed format.
slides.narration: This lecture explains APIs: endpoints, JSON as the common language, and how apps fetch data behind the scenes.

slides.heading: API basics
bullets: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules for programs to request data from each other.
An endpoint is a URL that does one job, like /users/42 returning user 42's profile.
JSON is the common data language: lightweight text both humans and programs can read.
Requests often carry keys or tokens proving who is asking. Never share yours.
Your weather app, your maps app, your social feed: all of them are API clients wearing a pretty interface.
slides.narration: APIs let programs order data like from a menu: endpoints name the dishes, JSON is the plating, and keys prove you may order.

slides.heading: JSON, the API language
slides.walkthrough: Curly braces mark an object: named values. Square brackets mark an array: an ordered list. Strings sit in quotes, numbers do not. This object has a name, a city, and a list of three scores.
slides.narration: JSON has two structures: objects for named values, arrays for ordered lists. Nearly every API response you will ever see is built from these.

slides.heading: An API call

diagram.title: An API call
diagram.note: Same request/response idea as the browser — but data instead of pages, and a program instead of a person reading it.

slides.narration: An API call mirrors a page load: request, response, display. The difference is that a program, not a person, consumes the answer.

slides.heading: Try it: design a call
slides.text: A weather app needs the forecast for Boston. Write down the endpoint it might call and sketch the JSON it might get back (city, temperature, condition).
slides.narration: Design an API call on paper: endpoint plus JSON shape. Thinking in endpoints and payloads is the core API skill.

tracks.title: Computer Hardware Basics
tracks.audience: Beginners who need the physical picture: what the CPU, RAM, and storage do and why their sizes matter.

slides.heading: CPU: the brain
slides.lede: The processor executes every instruction your computer runs. Cores and clock speed decide how fast.
slides.narration: This lecture explains the CPU: cores, clock speed, and the fetch-decode-execute cycle behind every computation.

slides.heading: The processor
bullets: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) executes machine instructions: the tiny steps every program is made of.
A core is an independent worker inside the CPU. Four cores can do four things truly at once.
Clock speed, measured in GHz (billions of cycles per second), says how fast each core works.
More cores means more parallelism; higher GHz means each task finishes sooner.
Cache is ultra-fast memory on the CPU itself, holding the data the current work needs most.
slides.narration: The CPU executes instructions; cores parallelize them; clock speed paces them. Cache keeps the hottest data within arm's reach.

slides.heading: Inside a CPU

diagram.title: Inside a CPU
diagram.note: Every core repeats the same cycle billions of times per second: fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it.

slides.narration: A CPU is cores, and each core is a relentless loop: fetch, decode, execute. Everything your computer does is this cycle, repeated.

slides.heading: Reading a spec line

code.code:
"8-core 3.2 GHz"
   |        |
   |        +-- each core ticks 3.2 billion times/sec
   +-- 8 workers running in parallel

twice the cores ~= twice the multitasking
twice the GHz   ~= each task finishes sooner

slides.walkthrough: 8-core means eight parallel workers. 3.2 GHz means each worker cycles 3.2 billion times per second. Marketing leans on both numbers because each measures a different kind of speed.
slides.narration: Spec lines decode cleanly: cores count parallelism, gigahertz counts pace. Neither alone tells the whole performance story.

slides.heading: Try it: check your cores
slides.text: Look up your own device's processor specs (search the model name plus specs). How many cores does it have, and what is its clock speed?
slides.narration: Find your own CPU's core count and speed. Reading real specs makes the abstract numbers concrete.

slides.heading: RAM versus storage
slides.lede: RAM is the desk; storage is the filing cabinet. You need both, for opposite reasons.
slides.narration: This lecture contrasts RAM and storage: speed versus permanence, and the size units from bytes to terabytes.

slides.heading: Two kinds of memory
bullets: RAM (Random Access Memory) is the fast workspace where running programs live. Power off and it forgets everything.
Storage (SSDs, hard drives) is the slow keeper: files survive reboots, but access takes longer.
Running programs and their data sit in RAM. Saved documents, photos, and the OS itself sit on storage.
More RAM means more programs open smoothly at once. More storage means more files kept.
SSDs are fast, silent storage with no moving parts. Hard drives are slower, cheaper per gigabyte.
slides.narration: RAM is fast and forgetful; storage is slow and permanent. Programs run in the first and are saved in the second.

slides.heading: RAM versus storage

diagram.title: RAM versus storage
diagram.note: When RAM fills up, the computer slows down. When storage fills up, you cannot save new files.

slides.narration: The tradeoff is speed and permanence against cost. Knowing which is full tells you whether to close apps or delete files.

slides.heading: The size ladder

code.code:
bit -> byte (8 bits) -> KB -> MB -> GB -> TB
each step is roughly 1000x the last

a text message  ~= a few KB
a photo         ~= 3 MB
a movie         ~= 2 GB
a laptop drive  ~= 512 GB

slides.walkthrough: Sizes climb in thousand-fold steps from bytes to terabytes. The examples anchor each unit: messages in kilobytes, photos in megabytes, movies in gigabytes, drives in hundreds of gigabytes.
slides.narration: Bytes scale in thousand-fold steps. Anchoring each unit to a familiar file — photo, movie, drive — makes sizes intuitive.

slides.heading: Try it: RAM or storage
slides.text: Two specs: 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB SSD. Which is the workspace and which is the filing cabinet? What happens when each one fills up?
slides.narration: Classify the two specs and predict the symptom of each filling up. This distinction resolves half of all my computer is slow complaints.

lectures.title: Bits, bytes, and why sizes matter

slides.heading: Bits, bytes, and why sizes matter
slides.lede: Everything digital is built from bits. Understand the bit-to-byte ladder and storage math stops being mysterious.
slides.narration: This lecture builds the size ladder from bits to megabytes, and connects it to the binary math module.

slides.heading: Bits and bytes
bullets: A bit is one binary digit: 0 or 1. It is the smallest possible piece of information.
A byte is 8 bits. One byte can represent 256 different values (0 through 255).
Roughly one byte stores one text character, which is why file sizes track character counts.
Computers count sizes in powers of two: 1 KB is 1024 bytes, not 1000.
The binary math module teaches the actual conversions step by step.
slides.narration: Bits are the atoms, bytes are the molecules: eight bits make a byte, and bytes stack into kilobytes in powers of two.

slides.heading: The binary size ladder

diagram.title: The binary size ladder
diagram.note: Storage math is powers of two. Marketers sometimes use 1000 instead of 1024, which is why drives seem smaller than advertised.

slides.narration: Each rung multiplies by 1024. The gap between marketing's 1000 and computing's 1024 explains the missing gigabytes on every new drive.

slides.heading: Worked: bytes in 2 KB

code.code:
1 KB = 1024 bytes
2 KB = 2 x 1024 = 2048 bytes

in bits: 2048 bytes x 8 = 16,384 bits

slides.walkthrough: Start from the definition: one kilobyte is 1024 bytes. Double it for two kilobytes: 2048 bytes. Each byte is 8 bits, so multiply by 8 for the bit count: 16,384 bits.
slides.narration: A worked conversion: kilobytes to bytes to bits, one multiplication at a time. The binary module practices this pattern until it is automatic.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: Bits (b) versus bytes (B). Network speeds are quoted in bits: 100 Mbps is about 12.5 megabytes per second.
Marketing gigabytes (1000-based) versus real gibibytes (1024-based). Your 1 TB drive holds about 931 GiB.
Confusing RAM gigabytes with disk gigabytes. 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of disk are different pools.
Assuming bigger numbers always win. A fast 8 GB machine can beat a slow 16 GB one.
slides.narration: The expensive confusions: bits versus bytes, marketing math versus real math, and RAM versus disk. All four are easy once named.

slides.heading: Try it: quick conversions
slides.text: How many bits are in 2 bytes? How many bytes in 3 KB? (Answers: 16 bits, 3072 bytes.) Then open the binary math module for the full workout.
slides.narration: Do two quick conversions by hand, then continue into the binary module where the arithmetic gets a full step-by-step treatment.

tracks.title: Security Basics
tracks.audience: Beginners entering any security-adjacent path: the CIA triad, threats versus vulnerabilities, and defense in depth.

slides.heading: The CIA triad
slides.lede: All of security serves three goals: keep secrets secret, keep data correct, and keep systems up.
slides.narration: This lecture introduces the CIA triad — confidentiality, integrity, availability — the three goals behind every security control.

slides.heading: Three goals
bullets: Confidentiality: only the right eyes see it. Passwords, encryption, and access controls serve this.
Integrity: data stays correct and trustworthy. Checksums, signatures, and audit logs serve this.
Availability: systems are there when needed. Backups, redundancy, and DDoS defenses serve this.
Every security control serves at least one of the three. Ask which one and the control's purpose becomes clear.
The three trade off: extreme secrecy can hurt availability, and vice versa. Balance is the job.
slides.narration: Confidentiality guards who sees, integrity guards what is true, availability guards whether it works. Every control serves at least one.

slides.heading: The triad

diagram.title: The triad
diagram.note: A breach of any one is a security incident. Strong security covers all three at once.
