slides.narration: Three pillars, one building. A leaked password breaks confidentiality, altered records break integrity, and an outage breaks availability.

slides.heading: Controls and their letters

code.code:
passwords        -> C (only you get in)
backups          -> A (restore after disaster)
checksums        -> I (detect tampering)
firewalls        -> C + A (block attackers, keep service up)
audit logs       -> I (prove what happened)

slides.walkthrough: Each control maps to the goal it serves. Passwords protect confidentiality, backups protect availability, checksums protect integrity. Firewalls serve two goals at once, which is common.
slides.narration: Mapping controls to letters turns a vocabulary list into a system: every tool you meet later will fit somewhere on this map.

slides.heading: Try it: which letter
slides.text: A bank's website goes down for an hour. Which leg of the triad broke? What about a leaked customer list, and silently altered transaction records?
slides.narration: Classify three incidents by triad leg. This classification is the first step of every incident report you will ever read.

slides.heading: Threats, vulnerabilities, and risk
slides.lede: Security vocabulary in one chain: a threat exploits a vulnerability, creating risk to something you care about.
slides.narration: This lecture defines threats, vulnerabilities, and risk — the three words every security conversation is built from.

slides.heading: The vocabulary
bullets: A threat is who or what could cause harm: criminals, malware, disgruntled insiders, natural disasters.
A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can exploit: unpatched software, weak passwords, unlocked doors.
An asset is what you protect: data, systems, reputation, people.
Risk is likelihood times impact: how probable the incident is, multiplied by how bad it would be.
Attack surface is everything exposed to threats: every open port, every login page, every employee.
slides.narration: Threats act, vulnerabilities allow, assets suffer, and risk measures the combination. Shrinking the attack surface shrinks them all.

slides.heading: The attack chain

diagram.title: The attack chain
diagram.note: Break any link — remove the threat's access, patch the weakness, protect the asset — and the incident never happens.

slides.narration: Every incident follows this chain: someone exploits something to hurt something. Defense means breaking the chain at its weakest link.

slides.heading: Risk as arithmetic

code.code:
risk = likelihood x impact

weak password on a test blog:
  likelihood high x impact low  = medium risk

weak password on the payroll system:
  likelihood high x impact high = critical risk

same weakness, different asset, different risk

slides.walkthrough: Risk multiplies two judgments: how likely and how bad. The same weak password is medium risk on a test blog but critical on payroll, because the asset's value changed the impact.
slides.narration: Risk is likelihood times impact. The same vulnerability carries different risk depending on what it guards — which is why asset value matters.

slides.heading: Try it: your laptop
slides.text: Name one threat, one vulnerability, and one asset for your own laptop. Then say which link in the chain you would break first.
slides.narration: Apply the vocabulary to your own machine. Personal examples make the abstract chain concrete.

slides.heading: Defense in depth
slides.lede: No single control is perfect. Security stacks layers so an attacker must beat every one.
slides.narration: This lecture teaches defense in depth: layered controls, least privilege, and the habits that make layers work.

slides.heading: Layers, not walls
bullets: Defense in depth stacks independent controls: if one fails, the next one catches the attacker.
Typical layers: physical (locked doors), network (firewalls), host (patches, antivirus), app (input checks), data (encryption), people (training).
Least privilege shrinks what each layer must defend: fewer permissions, smaller blast radius.
Patching closes known vulnerabilities before threats exploit them. Automate it where you can.
Backups are the last layer: when everything else fails, restore and carry on.
slides.narration: Layers turn single points of failure into a gauntlet. Each independent control forces the attacker to start over.

slides.heading: The layers

diagram.title: The layers
diagram.note: An attacker must beat every layer; defenders need only one layer to catch them.

slides.narration: Six layers from people to physical. The asymmetry favors defenders: the attacker needs a perfect run, you need a single catch.

slides.heading: Common pitfalls
bullets: We have a firewall, so we are safe. One layer is never the whole strategy.
Security through obscurity: hiding something is not protecting it. Assume attackers will find it.
Ignoring the human layer. Phishing beats firewalls because it targets people, not ports.
Set and forget. Unpatched layers rot: today's defense is next year's vulnerability.
slides.narration: The classic failures: trusting one layer, hiding instead of securing, forgetting people, and letting defenses rot unpatched.

slides.heading: Try it: protect your email
slides.text: List two layers currently protecting your email account (for example, a password and a second factor). What third layer could you add?
slides.narration: Audit your own email's layers. Seeing defense in depth in your own accounts makes the model stick.

tracks.title: Data Basics
tracks.audience: Beginners heading into data or database paths: what data is, types, keys, messy data, and asking questions of it.

slides.heading: Tables, types, and keys
slides.lede: Data is recorded facts. Types keep those facts honest, and keys keep them findable.
slides.narration: This lecture defines data, column types, primary keys, and NULL — the vocabulary of every database you will meet.

slides.heading: Data vocabulary
bullets: Data is recorded facts: names, prices, timestamps, measurements.
A type is a promise about what a column holds: text, numbers, dates, or true/false.
Types prevent nonsense: a date column rejects the word banana, catching errors early.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row, like an id no two records share.
NULL means missing or unknown. It is not zero and not an empty string — it is the absence of a value.
slides.narration: Types are promises that catch errors early; primary keys make rows findable; NULL honestly marks the unknown.

slides.heading: Data, organized

diagram.title: Data, organized
diagram.note: Databases hold tables, tables hold typed columns, columns hold rows of values. Types are enforced at the column level.

slides.narration: The organization ladder: database to table to typed column to row. Each level adds structure the level above relies on.

slides.heading: Types in a table

code.code:
orders
order_id  (number, primary key)
customer  (text)
order_date (date)
total     (number)
shipped   (true/false)

row: 101, "Alex", 2026-10-01, 49.99, true

slides.walkthrough: Five columns, five types. order_id is the primary key: unique per row. The sample row shows each type in action: a number, text in quotes, an ISO date, a decimal, and a boolean.
slides.narration: One table, five typed columns, one sample row. Reading a schema like this is the first skill of working with data.

slides.heading: Try it: type it
slides.text: For a playlist table, choose types for: song title, artist, duration in seconds, release date, and whether you liked it. Which column is the primary key?
slides.narration: Assign types to a playlist's columns and pick a primary key. Typing data well prevents entire categories of bugs.

slides.heading: Clean versus messy data
slides.lede: Real-world data arrives messy. Cleaning it — standardizing, deduping, validating — is most of the job.
slides.narration: This lecture covers messy data: the common defects, the cleaning process, and why garbage in means garbage out.

slides.heading: Why data is messy
bullets: Duplicates: the same customer entered twice with slightly different spelling.
Inconsistency: Boston, boston, and ' Boston ' are three spellings of one city.
Missing values: blank fields where data was never collected or was lost.
Wrong formats: dates as 10/4/26 in one row and Oct 4 2026 in another.
Garbage in, garbage out: analysis on messy data produces confident wrong answers.
slides.narration: Duplicates, inconsistent spelling, missing values, and mixed formats are the usual suspects. Analysis built on them lies with confidence.

slides.heading: The cleaning pipeline

diagram.title: The cleaning pipeline
diagram.note: Cleaning is usually most of the work on a data project. That is normal, not a sign of failure.

slides.narration: Cleaning is a pipeline: profile the raw data, fix what you find, validate the fixes, and only then analyze.

slides.heading: Before and after

code.code:
BEFORE (3 spellings, extra spaces):
"  Boston", "boston", "Boston "

AFTER (trimmed, one case):
"Boston", "Boston", "Boston"

now they match -> duplicates visible -> keep one

slides.walkthrough: Trimming spaces and standardizing case collapses three spellings into one. Only after standardizing can you see the duplicates — and only then can you safely remove them.
slides.narration: Standardize first, dedupe second: the order matters, because duplicates hide behind inconsistent formatting.

slides.heading: Try it: spot the mess
slides.text: This list has three problems — find them: ["NYC", "new york", "N Y C", "Boston", "boston"]. What would the cleaned list look like?
slides.narration: Find the inconsistencies in the messy list and write the cleaned version. Spotting mess is the first half of cleaning.

slides.heading: Asking questions of data
slides.lede: Data becomes answers when you ask well: count, group, and summarize until the pattern shows.
slides.narration: This lecture turns data into answers: aggregation with COUNT, grouping with GROUP BY, and the question-answer loop.

slides.heading: Questions into queries
bullets: A question becomes a query: how many customers per city is a COUNT grouped by city.
Aggregation summarizes many rows into one number: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
GROUP BY splits rows into buckets first, then aggregates each bucket separately.
Charts answer visually what tables answer numerically. The right chart makes patterns obvious.
Each answer suggests the next question. Data work is a loop, not a straight line.
slides.narration: Aggregation compresses rows into answers; grouping buckets them first. Questions, queries, and charts form a loop.

slides.heading: Counting per group
slides.walkthrough: GROUP BY city splits the rows into one bucket per city. COUNT(*) counts the rows in each bucket. The result has one row per city with its customer count — the answer to how many customers per city.
slides.narration: Group, then count: the single most useful query shape in data work. One statement answers a question a spreadsheet would take minutes to answer.

slides.heading: The data loop

diagram.title: The data loop
diagram.note: Decisions raise new questions, which restart the loop. Data work compounds.

slides.narration: Data work cycles: questions become queries, results become charts, charts inform decisions, and decisions raise sharper questions.

slides.heading: Try it: ask a question
slides.text: A store has an orders table with a total column. What business question does COUNT(*) answer about it? What about AVG(total)?
slides.narration: Match aggregations to business questions. Knowing which summary answers which question is the analyst's core instinct.
